claim: The mammalian auditory sensory epithelium has one of the most stereotyped cellular patterns known in vertebrates.
source: The mammalian auditory sensory epithelium has one of the most stereotyped cellular patterns known in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a general statement about the auditory sensory epithelium that draws on established scientific knowledge about cellular patterning in vertebrates.

claim: Mechano-sensory hair cells are arranged in precise rows, with one row of inner and three rows of outer hair cells spanning the length of the spiral-shaped sensory epithelium.
source: Mechano-sensory hair cells are arranged in precise rows, with one row of inner and three rows of outer hair cells spanning the length of the spiral-shaped sensory epithelium.
evidence: This describes the known anatomical arrangement of hair cells in the auditory sensory epithelium, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Differentiation of the auditory sensory epithelium is precisely timed and follows a steep longitudinal gradient.
source: Aiding such precise cellular patterning, differentiation of the auditory sensory epithelium is precisely timed and follows a steep longitudinal gradient.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is further supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A local gradient of Activin A signaling within the auditory sensory epithelium times the longitudinal gradient of hair cell differentiation.
source: Here, we identify Activin A and its antagonist follistatin as key regulators of hair cell differentiation and show, using mouse genetic approaches, that a local gradient of Activin A signaling within the auditory sensory epithelium times the longitudinal gradient of hair cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse genetic approaches presented in the manuscript, including FST overexpression and Inhba deletion experiments.

claim: Activin-type signaling regulates a radial gradient of terminal mitosis within the auditory sensory epithelium.
source: Furthermore, we provide evidence that Activin-type signaling regulates a radial gradient of terminal mitosis within the auditory sensory epithelium, which constitutes a novel mechanism for limiting the number of inner hair cells being produced.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation experiments showing differential timing of cell cycle exit between inner and outer hair cell progenitors.

claim: Auditory sensory progenitors exit the cell cycle in an apical-to-basal gradient.
source: Auditory sensory progenitors (pro-sensory cells) exit the cell cycle in an apical-to-basal gradient (Chen et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2006; Ruben, 1967)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hair cell differentiation occurs in an opposing, basal-to-apical gradient.
source: whereas their differentiation into hair cells and supporting cells occurs in an opposing, basal-to-apical gradient (Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling plays a key role in setting up the spatial and temporal pattern of auditory hair cell differentiation.
source: Recent studies uncovered that Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling plays a key role in setting up the spatial and temporal pattern of auditory hair cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pro-sensory cells are exposed to high concentrations of SHH protein secreted by the adjacent spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs).
source: In the undifferentiated cochlea, pro-sensory cells are exposed to high concentrations of SHH protein secreted by the adjacent spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) (Bok et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SGN-specific ablation of SHH or cochlear epithelial-specific ablation of Smoothened results in premature hair cell differentiation.
source: SGN-specific ablation of SHH or cochlear epithelial-specific ablation of its co-receptor Smoothened results in premature hair cell differentiation and in the most extreme case a reversal of the gradient of hair cell differentiation (Bok et al., 2013; Tateya et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ATOH1 is the earliest marker of nascent hair cells.
source: The basic-helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor ATOH1 is the earliest marker of nascent hair cells and is both necessary and sufficient for the production of hair cells (Bermingham et al., 1999; Cai et al., 2013; Woods et al., 2004; Zheng and Gao, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: ATOH1 is both necessary and sufficient for the production of hair cells.
source: The basic-helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor ATOH1 is the earliest marker of nascent hair cells and is both necessary and sufficient for the production of hair cells (Bermingham et al., 1999; Cai et al., 2013; Woods et al., 2004; Zheng and Gao, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: SHH signaling represses hair cell differentiation through maintaining the expression of HEY1 and HEY2 in pro-sensory cells.
source: SHH signaling represses hair cell differentiation, at least in part, through maintaining the expression of HEY1 and HEY2 in pro-sensory cells (Benito-Gonzalez and Doetzlhofer, 2014; Tateya et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HEY1 and HEY2 antagonize ATOH1 function.
source: The bHLH transcriptional repressors HEY1 and HEY2 have been shown to antagonize ATOH1 function (Doetzlhofer et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Loss of HEY1 and HEY2 leads to premature hair cell differentiation.
source: and their loss leads to premature hair cell differentiation (Benito-Gonzalez and Doetzlhofer, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Auditory pro-sensory cells express members of the inhibitor of differentiation (ID) family.
source: In addition to HEY1 and HEY2, auditory pro-sensory cells express members of the inhibitor of differentiation (ID) family (Jones et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: ID proteins are dominant negative regulators of bHLH transcription factors.
source: ID proteins are dominant negative regulators of bHLH transcription factors (reviewed in Wang and Baker, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: ID1-3 maintain pro-sensory cells in an undifferentiated state by interfering with ATOH1's ability to bind to DNA and auto-regulate its own expression.
source: Acting downstream of BMP signaling, ID1-3 are thought to maintain pro-sensory cells in an undifferentiated state by interfering with ATOH1's ability to bind to DNA and auto-regulate its own expression (Jones et al., 2006; Kamaid et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Id1-3 expression is downregulated in a subset of pro-sensory cells at the onset of differentiation.
source: Through a yet unknown mechanism, Id1-3 expression is downregulated in a subset of pro-sensory cells at the onset of differentiation, allowing these cells to upregulate ATOH1 and to differentiate into hair cells.
evidence: This statement combines established knowledge with an acknowledgment of an unknown mechanism.

claim: Over-activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling increases Atoh1 expression in differentiating cochlear explants.
source: Over-activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling has been shown to increase Atoh1 expression in differentiating cochlear explants, and in the absence of Wnt/β-catenin signaling hair cells fail to form (Jacques et al., 2012; Munnamalai and Fekete, 2016) (Shi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the absence of Wnt/β-catenin signaling hair cells fail to form.
source: Over-activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling has been shown to increase Atoh1 expression in differentiating cochlear explants, and in the absence of Wnt/β-catenin signaling hair cells fail to form (Jacques et al., 2012; Munnamalai and Fekete, 2016) (Shi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The pattern of Wnt–reporter activity does not parallel the basal-to-apical wave of differentiation.
source: However, the pattern of Wnt–reporter activity, which at the onset of hair cell differentiation is high in the cochlear apex but low in the cochlear base, does not parallel the basal-to-apical wave of differentiation (Jacques et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The Inhba gene is expressed in a basal-to-apical gradient within the differentiating auditory sensory epithelium.
source: Interestingly, the Inhba gene, which encodes the Activin A subunit Inhibin βA (Barton et al., 1989), has been recently reported to be expressed in a basal-to-apical gradient within the differentiating auditory sensory epithelium (Son et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activins belong to the transforming growth factor (TGF)-β superfamily of cytokines.
source: Activins, which belong to the transforming growth factor (TGF)-β superfamily of cytokines, control a broad range of biological processes, including reproduction, embryonic axial specification, organogenesis and adult tissue homeostasis (reviewed in Namwanje and Brown, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the classification of Activins, supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Activins control a broad range of biological processes, including reproduction, embryonic axial specification, organogenesis and adult tissue homeostasis.
source: Activins, which belong to the transforming growth factor (TGF)-β superfamily of cytokines, control a broad range of biological processes, including reproduction, embryonic axial specification, organogenesis and adult tissue homeostasis (reviewed in Namwanje and Brown, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Canonical TGFβ-type signaling is transduced by receptor regulated SMAD proteins (R-SMADs).
source: Canonical TGFβ-type signaling is transduced by receptor regulated SMAD proteins (R-SMADs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TGFβ signaling mechanisms.

claim: Upon receptor mediated phosphorylation, R-SMADs form heteromeric complexes with SMAD4, which enables them to translocate to the nucleus and activate target genes.
source: Upon receptor mediated phosphorylation, R-SMADs (SMAD1, 2, 3, 5, 9) form heteromeric complexes with SMAD4, which enables them to translocate to the nucleus and activate a broad array of target genes (reviewed in Massagué, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article and represents established knowledge.

claim: In the developing spinal cord, Activins and other TGF-β-related ligands are required for Atoh1 induction in dorsally located neuronal progenitors.
source: In the developing spinal cord, Activins and other TGF-β-related ligands are required in most dorsally located neuronal progenitors for Atoh1 induction and their subsequent differentiation as D1A/B commissural neurons (Lee et al., 1998; Wine-Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At stage E13.5, Atoh1 expression starts in a subset of Sox2 positive pro-sensory cells at the basal turn of the cochlea.
source: In mice, Atoh1 expression starts around embryonic stage E13.5-E14.0 in a subset of Sox2 positive pro-sensory cells at the basal turn of the cochlea (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Inhba expression parallels Atoh1 expression and is limited to the basal pro-sensory domain at E13.5.
source: Paralleling Atoh1 expression, Inhba expression was limited to the basal pro-sensory domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fst is highly expressed within the lateral part of the pro-sensory domain throughout the cochlear apex and mid turn but is only weakly expressed in the cochlear base at E13.5.
source: In contrast, Fst was highly expressed within the lateral part of the pro-sensory domain throughout the cochlear apex and mid turn but was only weakly expressed in the cochlear base.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: As hair cell differentiation progresses towards the cochlear apex, Inhba expression within the pro-sensory/sensory domain extends to the cochlear mid-turn at E14.5 and E15.5.
source: At stages E14.5 and E15.5, as hair cell differentiation progressed towards the cochlear apex, Inhba expression within the pro-sensory/sensory domain extended to the cochlear mid-turn (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Fst expression regresses in the cochlear base and weakens in the cochlear mid-turn but continues to be highly expressed in the undifferentiated cochlear apex at E14.5 and E15.5.
source: At the same time, Fst expression further regressed in the cochlear base and weakened in the cochlear mid-turn but continued to be highly expressed in the undifferentiated cochlear apex.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Pro-sensory cells in the differentiating cochlea are exposed to an Activin A signaling gradient that closely resembles the spatial and temporal pattern of hair cell differentiation.
source: As summarized in Figure 1D, our analysis of Inhba and Fst expression suggests that pro-sensory cells in the differentiating cochlea are exposed to an Activin A signaling gradient that closely resembles the spatial and temporal pattern of hair cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the expression patterns of Inhba and Fst shown in Figure 1.

claim: Activins play a central role in coordinating growth and differentiation in sensory and neuronal tissues, including the retina, olfactory epithelium and spinal cord.
source: Activins play a central role in coordinating growth and differentiation in sensory and neuronal tissues, including the retina, olfactory epithelium and spinal cord (Davis et al., 2000; Gokoffski et al., 2011; Liem et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activin A treatment promotes precocious hair cell differentiation in E13.5 cochlear explants.
source: After 12 hr of culture, control cultures showed no or only weak Atoh1-GFP-reporter activity (GFP) within the developing cochlear duct (Figure 2B, Control, 12 hr). By contrast, a narrow stripe of GFP positive inner hair cells was already evident in Activin A-treated cochlear explants (Figure 2B, Activin A, 12 hr).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The band of GFP positive cells extends further apically in Activin A-treated cochlear explants compared to control cochlear explants.
source: Furthermore, at all stages examined, the band of GFP positive cells extended further apically in Activin A-treated cochlear explants compared to control cochlear explants (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Activin A acts as a differentiation signal for auditory hair cells.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that Activin A acts a differentiation signal for auditory hair cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing precocious hair cell differentiation in response to Activin A treatment.

claim: Activin A treatment increases the expression of Atoh1 by more than 4-fold.
source: We found that Activin A treatment increased the expression of Atoh1 and the Wnt-target gene Lgr5 by more than 4-fold
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Activin A treatment increases the expression of Lgr5 by more than 4-fold.
source: We found that Activin A treatment increased the expression of Atoh1 and the Wnt-target gene Lgr5 by more than 4-fold
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Activin A treatment increases the expression of Pou4f3 by more than 12-fold.
source: and increased the expression of Pou4f3, a critical early hair cell-specific transcription factor by more than 12-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Activin treatment leads to a more than 2-fold reduction in Bmp4, Id2, Id3 and Id4 expression.
source: Furthermore, Activin treatment led to a more than 2-fold reduction in Bmp4, Id2, Id3 and Id4 expression
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Activin treatment does not significantly alter the expression of p27/Kip1, Etv5, Hey1, Hey2, Fgf20 and Ptch1.
source: but did not significantly alter the expression of other pro-sensory genes (p27/Kip1- official gene name Cdkn1b, Etv5, Hey1, Hey2, Fgf20 and Ptch1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: BMP receptor signaling positively regulates Id1-3 expression in cochlear and vestibular pro-sensory cells.
source: BMP receptor signaling has been shown to positively regulate Id1-3 expression in cochlear and vestibular pro-sensory cells (Kamaid et al., 2010; Ohyama et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Brief BMP4 treatment significantly increases Id1 and Id3 expression but has no effect on Id4 and Atoh1 expression.
source: Brief BMP4 treatment significantly increased Id1 and Id3 expression compared to control but had no effect on Id4 and Atoh1 expression (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Brief Activin A treatment results in a modest but significant decrease in Id4 expression but does not alter Id1-3 or Atoh1 expression.
source: Conversely, the brief Activin A treatment resulted in a modest, but significant decrease in Id4 expression compared to control but did not alter Id1-3 or Atoh1 expression (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Activin A selectively stimulates the phosphorylation of SMAD2/3 in the developing cochlea.
source: Indeed, we found that in the developing cochlea Activin A selectively stimulated the phosphorylation of SMAD2/3, whereas BMP4 treatment selectively induced the phosphorylation of SMAD1/5/9 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: BMP4 treatment selectively induces the phosphorylation of SMAD1/5/9 in the developing cochlea.
source: Indeed, we found that in the developing cochlea Activin A selectively stimulated the phosphorylation of SMAD2/3, whereas BMP4 treatment selectively induced the phosphorylation of SMAD1/5/9 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Activin A positively regulates Atoh1 expression through an indirect mechanism that involves the repression of BMP-dependent and independent Id gene expression.
source: Taken together these findings suggests that Activin A positively regulates Atoh1 expression through an indirect mechanism that, at least in part, involves the repression of BMP-dependent and independent Id gene expression.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing differential effects of Activin A on Id gene expression.

claim: FST overexpressing cochlear tissue lacks hair cells at E14.5 while control cochlear tissue already contains inner hair cells at the base of the cochlea.
source: While control cochlear tissue already contained inner hair cells at the base of the cochlea, as shown here using cochlear whole mounts and sections, FST overexpressing cochlear tissue still lacked hair cells (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FST overexpression experiments shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Atoh1 and Pou4f3 mRNA expression is significantly reduced in E14.5 FST overexpressing cochlear epithelia.
source: Consistent with FST antagonizing hair cell differentiation, we found that Atoh1 and Pou4f3 mRNA expression was significantly reduced in E14.5 FST overexpressing cochlear epithelia
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Id3 and Id4 mRNA expression is significantly increased in E14.5 FST overexpressing cochlear epithelia compared to control.
source: whereas the mRNA expression of Id3 and Id4 was significantly increased compared to control (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: FST overexpression results in a modest but significant increase in the expression of Ptch1 and Etv5.
source: In addition, FST overexpression resulted in a modest but significant increase in the expression of the SHH receptor encoding gene Ptch1 (Driver et al., 2008) and the FGFR target and effector gene Etv5 (Hayashi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E and citations to previous studies.

claim: The expression of Fgf20, Hey1 and Hey2 remains unchanged in response to FST overexpression.
source: Despite these changes, the expression of Fgf20, Hey1 and Hey2, which are targets and effectors of SHH/FGFR signaling (Benito-Gonzalez and Doetzlhofer, 2014; Tateya et al., 2013), remained unchanged in response to FST overexpression (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E and citations to previous studies.

claim: FST overexpression leads to a modest but significant reduction in the expression of Bmp4.
source: Interestingly, FST overexpression also led to a modest but significant reduction in the expression of Bmp4.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: FST overexpression significantly reduces P-SMAD2/3 protein levels in the developing cochlea.
source: Consistent with its role as a canonical Activin antagonist, overexpression of FST significantly reduced P-SMAD2/3 protein levels in the developing cochlea.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: Cochlear P-SMAD1/5/9 protein levels remain unchanged in response to FST overexpression.
source: By contrast, cochlear P-SMAD1/5/9 protein levels, a readout for BMP signaling, remained unchanged in response to FST overexpression (Figure 3F,G)
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: FST overexpression does not disrupt BMP signaling in the developing cochlea.
source: suggesting that FST overexpression does not disrupt BMP signaling in the developing cochlea.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the Western blot data showing unchanged P-SMAD1/5/9 levels.

claim: Hair cell differentiation occurs significantly earlier in Activin A-treated wild type cochlear explants compared to untreated wild type cochlear explants.
source: Consistent with our earlier findings, we observed that hair cell differentiation occurred significantly earlier in Activin A-treated wild type cochlear explants compared to untreated wild type cochlear explants (Figure 4B,C,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures shown in Figures 4B, 4C, and 4F.

claim: The onset of hair cell differentiation is significantly delayed in untreated FST overexpressing cochlear explants compared to untreated wild type cochlear explants.
source: Conversely, the onset of hair cell differentiation was significantly delayed in untreated FST overexpressing cochlear explants compared to untreated wild type cochlear explants (Figure 4B,D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures shown in Figures 4B, 4D, and 4F.

claim: Activin A treatment rescues the FST-mediated delay in hair cell differentiation.
source: These defects were almost completely abolished when Activin A treatment and FST overexpression were combined and no significant differences in the onset or in the progression of hair cell differentiation was observed between FST overexpressing cochlear explants treated with Activin A and wild type untreated cochlear explants (Figure 4B,E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures shown in Figures 4B, 4E, and 4F.

claim: FST antagonizes hair cell differentiation in an Activin A-dependent manner.
source: In summary, our data suggest that FST antagonizes hair cell differentiation in an Activin A-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the rescue experiments showing that Activin A can overcome FST-mediated delays.

claim: Induction of FST overexpression at E11.5 or E14.5 results in neonatal lethality of R26-FST transgenic animals.
source: Induction of FST overexpression at E11.5 or as late as E14.5 resulted in neonatal lethality of R26-FST transgenic animals, limiting our analysis to late embryonic stages.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedures.

claim: R26-FST cochlear tissue contains two rows of inner hair cells throughout the basal half of the cochlea at E18.5.
source: By contrast, R26-FST cochlear tissue contained two rows of inner hair cells throughout the basal half of the cochlea (Figure 5A,B, R26-FST).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The density of inner phalangeal cells is similarly increased in response to FST overexpression.
source: The observed ectopic inner hair cells were unlikely to be the product of supporting cell-to-hair cell fate conversion, as the density of supporting cells that surrounded inner hair cells-called inner phalangeal cells- was similarly increased in response to FST overexpression (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The outer hair cell density and cellular patterning is unchanged in response to FST overexpression except for the cochlear base.
source: Interestingly, the outer hair cell density and cellular patterning was unchanged in response to FST overexpression except for the cochlear base.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The base of FST overexpressing cochleae contains short stretches of sensory epithelium in which the third row of outer hair cells is missing.
source: The base of FST overexpressing cochleae contained short stretches of sensory epithelium in which the third row of outer hair cells was missing, resulting in a modest reduction in outer hair cell density (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Differentiation/maturation of the auditory sensory epithelium is severely delayed in response to FST overexpression.
source: Furthermore, differentiation/maturation of the auditory sensory epithelium was severely delayed in response to FST overexpression.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple observations including delayed stereocilia formation and reduced cochlear length.

claim: Auditory sensory epithelia from R26-FST transgenic animals are 30% shorter compared to auditory sensory epithelia from control littermates at E18.5.
source: Consistent with a severe delay in hair cell differentiation, auditory sensory epithelia from R26-FST transgenic animals had not yet thinned to a single layer of supporting cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and their length was 30% shorter compared to auditory sensory epithelia from control littermates (single transgenic control = 5.14 ± 0.04 mm, R26-FST = 3.65 ± 0.13 mm, n = 5, p=0.0002).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Hair cells in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue have less mature stereocilia than their wild type counterparts at E18.5.
source: Moreover, hair cells in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue had less mature stereocilia than their wild type counterparts, and apical hair cells lacked stereocilia completely (Figure 5B, R26-FST).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: FST induction at E13.0 has no effect on the length of the auditory sensory epithelium at E17.5.
source: FST induction one day later at ~E13.0 (dox E12.5), had no effect on the length of the auditory sensory epithelium (dox E12.5, harvest E17.5: single transgenic control = 4.13 ± 0.17 mm, R26-FST = 3.99 ± 0.12 mm, n = 3, p=0.5425).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Ectopic inner hair cells continue to be observed when FST is induced at E13.0, with the highest number found in the basal portion of the auditory sensory epithelium.
source: However, we continued to observe ectopic inner hair cells in FST overexpressing cochleae, with the highest number of ectopic hair cells found in the basal portion of the auditory sensory epithelium, as well as short stretches of sensory epithelium with only two rows of outer hair cells (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: FST induction as late as E13.0 causes a delay in hair cell differentiation/maturation.
source: Furthermore, we found that hair cell stereocilia in FST overexpressing cochleae had a less mature phenotype compared to their counterparts in control cochlear tissue, indicating that FST induction as late as ~E13.0 causes a delay in hair cells differentiation/maturation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The conditional knockout of the Inhba gene does not alter overall cochlear morphology or the length of the sensory epithelium at P0.
source: The conditional knockout (cKO) of the Inhba gene did not alter overall cochlear morphology, nor did it alter the length of the sensory epithelium compared to control (Inhba fl/fl) (P0: control = 4.99 ± 0.12 mm; Inhba cKO = 4. 82 ± 0.01 mm; n = 2, p-value=0.4043).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Loss of Inhba gene function results in hair cell maturation and patterning defects.
source: However, as predicted, loss of Inhba gene function resulted in hair cell maturation and patterning defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Inhba conditional knockout mice.

claim: Inhba cKO cochlear tissue shows a significant increase in the number of ectopic inner hair cells compared to control.
source: By contrast, Inhba cKO cochlear tissue showed a significant increase in the number of ectopic inner hair cells compared to control, with more of the ectopic inner hair cells residing within the most basal segment (Figure 6C, Inhba cKO, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Hair cell stereocilia in Inhba mutant cochlear tissue have a less mature phenotype compared to their counterparts in control cochlear tissue.
source: Furthermore, consistent with a delayed onset of hair cell differentiation, hair cell stereocilia in the base, mid and apex of Inhba mutant cochlear tissue had a less mature phenotype compared to their counterparts in control cochlear tissue (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Inhba (Activin A) function is required for limiting inner hair cell formation and for timing hair cell differentiation/maturation in vivo.
source: Taken together, our findings demonstrate that Inhba (Activin A) function is required for limiting inner hair cell formation as well as for timing hair cell differentiation/maturation in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data from Inhba conditional knockout mice.

claim: FST likely disrupts other Activin-related signaling mechanisms in addition to Activin A signaling in the developing cochlea.
source: The milder defects in cochlear hair cell formation observed in Inhba mutants suggest that in addition to Activin A signaling, FST likely disrupts other, Activin-related signaling mechanisms in the developing cochlea.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing the phenotypes of FST overexpression and Inhba deletion.

claim: Activin B (Inhbb), GDF11 and Myostatin (Mstn) activate SMAD2/3 signaling and are high affinity binding partners of FST.
source: Like Activin A, Activin B (Inhbb) and the Activin-related ligands GDF11 and Myostatin (Mstn) activate SMAD2/3 signaling and are high affinity binding partners of FST (Thompson et al., 2005; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gdf11 transcript is abundantly expressed at the onset of and during cochlear differentiation.
source: We found Gdf11 transcript to be abundantly expressed at the onset of (E13.5) as well as during (E14.5, E15.5) cochlear differentiation, making it a likely candidate for FST-mediated regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhbb and Mstn transcripts are undetectable or expressed at very low levels in the developing cochlear epithelial duct.
source: By contrast, Inhbb and Mstn transcripts were undetectable or expressed at very low levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the murine cochlea, cell cycle exit occurs within a 48 hr time window, with apically located pro-sensory cells exiting as early as E12.5 and basal pro-sensory cells exiting as late as E14.5.
source: In the murine cochlea, cell cycle exit occurs within a 48 hr time window, with apically located pro-sensory cells exiting the cell cycle as early as E12.5 and pro-sensory cells located in the base of the cochlea exiting as late as E14.5 (Lee et al., 2006; Ruben, 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hair cells located in the basal turn of the cochlea incorporate EdU at high rate (~25%) in both control and R26-FST transgenic animals when EdU is administered at E13.5.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we found that hair cells located in the basal turn of the cochlea incorporated EdU at high rate (~25%) in both control and R26-FST transgenic animals (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figures 7A-C.

claim: Control cochlear hair cells located in the mid and apex show little to no EdU incorporation when EdU is administered at E13.5, while their counterparts in FST overexpressing cochleae exhibit robust EdU incorporation.
source: However, while control cochlear hair cells located further apically (mid and apex) showed little to no EdU incorporation, their counterparts in FST overexpressing cochleae exhibited robust EdU incorporation (Figure 7A–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figures 7A-C.

claim: FST overexpression in the developing cochlea delays pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal.
source: indicating that FST overexpression in the developing cochlea delays pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EdU incorporation data.

claim: FST overexpression does not disrupt the apical-to-basal gradient of pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal.
source: FST overexpression did not disrupt the apical-to-basal gradient of pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EdU incorporation data showing that apical hair cells still incorporate EdU at lower rates than basal hair cells in FST overexpressing tissue.

claim: In wild type cochlear tissue, inner hair cell progenitors withdraw from the cell cycle prior to outer hair cell progenitor cells.
source: Interestingly, our analysis revealed that in wild type cochlear tissue inner and outer hair cell progenitors did not withdraw from the cell cycle at the same time. We found that in the mid-turn of control cochleae more than 6% of outer hair cells were labeled with EdU, whereas no EdU incorporation was found in inner hair cells, suggesting that inner hair cell progenitors had exited the cell cycle prior to the more laterally located outer hair cell progenitors (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: No difference in the frequency of EdU incorporation among inner and outer hair cells is observed in FST overexpressing cochleae.
source: By contrast, no difference in the frequency of EdU incorporation among inner and outer hair cells was observed in FST overexpressing cochleae (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Supporting cells and hair cells in R26-FST transgenic animals incorporate EdU at much higher frequency than their counterparts in control animals when EdU is administered daily from E14.5 to E17.5.
source: Again, consistent with a severe delay in pro-sensory cell cycle exit, supporting cells and hair cells in R26-FST transgenic animals incorporated EdU at much higher frequency than their counterparts in control (single transgenic) animals (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figures 8A-D.

claim: In control cochlear tissue, the percentage of outer hair cells that incorporated EdU (12.1%) is significantly higher compared to the percentage of inner hair cells that incorporated EdU (1.5%).
source: In control cochlear tissue, consistent with the existence of a medial-to-lateral gradient of cell cycle withdrawal, the percentage of outer hair cells (12.1%) that incorporated EdU was significantly higher compared to the percentage of inner hair cells (1.5%) that incorporated EdU (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: In FST overexpressing cochlear tissue, inner hair cells incorporate EdU at a similar or higher rate than outer hair cells.
source: By contrast, in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue, inner hair cells incorporated EdU at a similar or higher rate than outer hair cells (Figure 8F)
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: In the apex of FST overexpressing cochlear tissue, inner hair cells and their surrounding inner phalangeal cells are the only cell types labeled with EdU.
source: and in its apex inner hair cells and their surrounding inner phalangeal cells were the only cell types that were labeled with EdU (Figure 8A,B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figures 8A, 8B, and 8D.

claim: The ectopic hair cells observed in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue are, at least in part, the product of prolonged proliferation of inner hair cell progenitor cells.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the ectopic hair cells observed in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue are, at least in part, the product of prolonged proliferation of inner hair cell progenitor cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EdU incorporation data showing prolonged proliferation of inner hair cell progenitors.

claim: Activin A acts as a pro-differentiation signal in the mammalian cochlea.
source: We find that exogenous Activin A triggers premature hair cell differentiation in cochlear explant cultures and demonstrate that disruption of Activin A signaling due to FST overexpression or Inhba deletion results in a delay in cochlear hair cell differentiation in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures and genetic manipulations.

claim: Activin signaling promotes cortical interneuron differentiation through the inhibition of SHH signaling.
source: For instance, Activin signaling has been shown to promote cortical interneuron differentiation, at least in part, through the inhibition of SHH signaling (Cambray et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Neither over-activation nor loss of Activin signaling alters the expression of SHH target and effector genes Hey1, Hey2 and Fgf20.
source: However, we found no evidence for direct interference as neither over-activation nor loss of Activin signaling altered the expression of SHH target and effector genes Hey1, Hey2 and Fgf20 (Benito-Gonzalez and Doetzlhofer, 2014; Tateya et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Activin signaling does not activate Atoh1 expression directly but rather through indirect mechanisms.
source: However, a brief 4 hr Activin A treatment failed to significantly increase Atoh1 transcript abundance, suggesting that Activin signaling does not activate Atoh1 expression directly but rather through indirect mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing no immediate increase in Atoh1 expression after brief Activin A treatment.

claim: Activin signaling positively regulates ATOH1 activity/expression through inhibiting cochlear expression of Id3 and Id4.
source: Indeed, our findings suggest that Activin signaling positively regulates ATOH1 activity/expression through inhibiting cochlear expression of Id3 and Id4.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing reduced Id3 and Id4 expression in response to Activin A treatment.

claim: A failure to downregulate Id3 expression in hair cell progenitors inhibits the formation of hair cells in both auditory and vestibular sensory organs.
source: Consistent with an inhibitory role in hair cell differentiation, previous studies found that a failure to downregulate Id3 expression in hair cell progenitors inhibits the formation of hair cells in both auditory and vestibular sensory organs (Jones et al., 2006; Kamaid et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Atoh1 expression and subsequent hair cell differentiation is delayed but not disrupted in response to FST overexpression or Inhba ablation.
source: It should be noted that Atoh1 expression and subsequent hair cell differentiation is not disrupted, but rather delayed in response to FST overexpression or Inhba ablation, suggesting the existence of Activin-independent mechanisms capable of activating Atoh1 expression in pro-sensory cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: The Wnt effector β-catenin is required for hair cell specification and has been shown to directly activate Atoh1 transcription in neuronal progenitors.
source: The Wnt effector β-catenin is required for hair cell specification and has been shown to directly activate Atoh1 transcription in neuronal progenitors (Shi et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling initiates Atoh1 expression, whereas Activin signaling functions to enhance Atoh1 expression/activity along the longitudinal cochlear axis.
source: Taking these recent findings and our findings into consideration, we propose a model in which Wnt/β-catenin signaling initiates Atoh1 expression, whereas Activin signaling functions to enhance Atoh1 expression/activity along the longitudinal cochlear axis.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on inference from the current findings and previous studies.

claim: Early SHH signaling from the ventral midline is critical for establishing regional identity in the developing cochlea, including the distinct basal–apical pattern of Inhba and Fst expression.
source: Early SHH signaling, presumably from the ventral midline, is critical for establishing regional identity in the developing cochlea, including setting up the distinct basal–apical pattern of Inhba and Fst expression.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and inference.

claim: Subsequent SHH signaling from the spiral ganglion is dispensable for establishing/maintaining Inhba and Fst expression.
source: However, subsequent SHH signaling from the spiral ganglion is dispensable for establishing/maintaining Inhba and Fst expression (Son et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Notch signaling positively regulates Inhba expression in differentiating and terminal differentiated supporting cells.
source: Notch signaling is active in pro-sensory cells and has been shown to positively regulate Inhba expression in differentiating and terminal differentiated supporting cells (Campbell et al., 2016; Maass et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FST overexpression delays the onset of pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal and differentiation.
source: We show that FST overexpression delays the onset of pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal and differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from EdU incorporation experiments.

claim: LIN28B plays a similar function to FST in timing pro-sensory cell withdrawal and differentiation.
source: A similar function in timing pro-sensory cell withdrawal and differentiation has been recently reported for the RNA binding protein LIN28B (Golden et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The expression of Fst in the developing cochlea largely mimics that of Lin28b.
source: Interestingly, the expression of Fst in the developing cochlea largely mimics that of Lin28b; each are initially highly expressed in pro-sensory cells and are downregulated upon differentiation following a basal-to-apical gradient.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of expression patterns from the current study and previous studies.

claim: TGF-β-related signaling pathways inhibit proliferation through promoting the expression and/or activity of cyclin dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitors.
source: TGF-β-related signaling pathways are known to inhibit proliferation through promoting the expression and/or activity of cyclin dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitors (Massagué and Gomis, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and represents established knowledge.

claim: The CDK inhibitor p27/Kip1 (CDKN1B) is the main regulator of pro-sensory cell cycle exit in the developing cochlea.
source: In the developing cochlea, the CDK inhibitor p27/Kip1 (CDKN1B) is the main regulator of pro-sensory cell cycle exit and its transcriptional upregulation directs the apical-to-basal wave of pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal (Chen and Segil, 1999; Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: No changes in p27/Kip1 mRNA expression are observed in response to FST overexpression.
source: However, we observed no changes in p27/Kip1 mRNA expression in response to FST overexpression
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The observed delay in pro-sensory cell cycle exit may be due to a reduction in p27/Kip1 protein stability and/or activity.
source: suggesting that the observed delay in pro-sensory cell cycle exit may instead be due to a reduction in p27/Kip1 protein stability and/or activity.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The increase in Id3 and Id4 expression in response to FST overexpression likely contributed to the observed delay in pro-sensory cell cycle exit.
source: In addition, it is likely that the increase in Id3 and Id4 expression in response to FST overexpression contributed to the observed delay in pro-sensory cell cycle exit.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the experimental data and established knowledge about ID proteins.

claim: High ID protein expression is associated with a proliferative, undifferentiated cell state.
source: High ID protein expression is associated with a proliferative, undifferentiated cell state and ID4 expression in spermatogonia and mammary glands is a predictor for stemness (Helsel et al., 2017; Wang and Baker, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fst can be detected within the most ventral aspect of the developing otocyst as early as E10.5, preceding Activin A expression by several days.
source: This is quite likely as Fst can be detected within the most ventral aspect of the developing otocyst as early as E10.5, preceding Activin A expression by several days (Son et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The cochlear defects observed in Inhba mutants are much milder compared to the cochlear defects observed in FST transgenic animals.
source: Furthermore, the cochlear defects observed in Inhba mutants are much milder compared to the cochlear defects observed in FST transgenic animals.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental data from Inhba mutants and FST transgenic animals.

claim: GDF11 is the predominant Activin-type ligand within the developing cochlea.
source: A potential candidate is GDF11, which our qPCR-based expression analysis identified as the predominant Activin-type ligand within the developing cochlea.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: GDF11–FST axis regulates progenitor cell proliferation and differentiation in various sensory tissues.
source: GDF11–FST axis has been shown to regulate progenitor cell proliferation and differentiation in various sensory tissues (Beites et al., 2009; Gokoffski et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In adult chicken auditory sensory epithelia, disruption of Activin signaling attenuates the low rate of regenerative cell proliferation.
source: In adult chicken auditory sensory epithelia disruption of Activin signaling attenuates the low rate of regenerative cell proliferation, whereas exogenous Activin A stimulates cell proliferation (McCullar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In adult chicken auditory sensory epithelia, exogenous Activin A stimulates cell proliferation.
source: In adult chicken auditory sensory epithelia disruption of Activin signaling attenuates the low rate of regenerative cell proliferation, whereas exogenous Activin A stimulates cell proliferation (McCullar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: FST overexpression results in an overproduction of inner hair cells.
source: We find that FST overexpression and to a lesser extent ablation of Activin A (Inhba) results in an overproduction of inner hair cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FST overexpression and Inhba ablation experiments.

claim: Ablation of Activin A (Inhba) results in an overproduction of inner hair cells to a lesser extent than FST overexpression.
source: We find that FST overexpression and to a lesser extent ablation of Activin A (Inhba) results in an overproduction of inner hair cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FST overexpression and Inhba ablation experiments.

claim: In certain tissues, including the developing tongue, FST interferes with BMP signaling.
source: In certain tissues, including the developing tongue, FST has been shown to interfere with BMP signaling (Beites et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the mammalian cochlea, BMP-receptor signaling is critical for the specification of sensory and non-sensory territories and the medial-lateral partitioning of the pro-sensory domain.
source: In the mammalian cochlea BMP-receptor signaling is critical for the specification of sensory and non-sensory territories and the medial-lateral partitioning of the pro-sensory domain (Ohyama et al., 2010) (Munnamalai and Fekete, 2016; Puligilla et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FST overexpression does not disrupt or significantly reduce BMP signaling within the developing cochlea.
source: However, we found no evidence that FST overexpression disrupted or significantly reduced BMP signaling within the developing cochlea.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing unchanged P-SMAD1/5/9 levels and Id1-3 expression.

claim: The ectopic inner hair cells in FST transgenic and Inhba mutant animals are the product of prolonged inner hair cell progenitor proliferation.
source: Instead, we propose that the ectopic inner hair cells in FST transgenic and Inhba mutant animals are the product of prolonged inner hair cell progenitor proliferation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on inference from the EdU incorporation data.

claim: Under normal conditions, inner hair cell progenitors withdraw from the cell cycle prior to outer hair cell progenitor cells.
source: We show that under normal conditions inner hair cell progenitors withdraw from the cell cycle prior to outer hair cell progenitor cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data.

claim: The distinct medial-to-lateral gradient of terminal mitosis is lost in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that this distinct medial-to-lateral gradient of terminal mitosis is lost in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue, resulting in a disproportional increase in inner hair cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data.

claim: At the peak of terminal mitosis (E13.5), Fst expression becomes restricted to the lateral portion of the pro-sensory domain.
source: We show that at the peak of terminal mitosis (E13.5), Fst expression becomes restricted to the lateral portion of the pro-sensory domain
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: Inner hair cell progenitors experience higher levels of Activin-type signaling than more laterally located outer hair cell progenitor cells.
source: suggesting that inner hair cell progenitors experience higher levels of Activin-type signaling (Activin A, GDF11) than more laterally located outer hair cell progenitor cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the expression patterns of Fst and Inhba.

claim: The radial gradient of terminal mitosis constitutes a novel mechanism for limiting the number of inner hair cells being produced in the mammalian cochlea.
source: This newly identified radial gradient of terminal mitosis constitutes a novel mechanism for limiting the number of inner hair cells that are being produced in the mammalian cochlea.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Two FST molecules encircle the Inhibin β dimer, blocking both type I and type II receptor binding sites.
source: Two FST molecules encircle the Inhibin β dimer, blocking both type I and type II receptor binding sites, thus preventing receptor binding and activation of its downstream signaling cascade (Thompson et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and represents established knowledge about FST mechanism.

claim: Within the differentiating auditory sensory epithelium, Fst and Inhba are expressed in opposing gradients.
source: Within the differentiating auditory sensory epithelium Fst and the Inhibin βA encoding gene Inhba are expressed in opposing gradients, with Inhba being highest expressed within the basal sensory epithelium and Fst being highest expressed apically (Son et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hair cell differentiation follows a steep basal-to-apical gradient in which hair cells in the cochlear mid-basal segment differentiate prior to more apically located hair cells.
source: Hair cell differentiation follows a steep basal-to-apical gradient in which hair cells located within the cochlear mid-basal segment differentiate prior to more apically located hair cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair cell differentiation patterns.

claim: A shallower, medial-to-lateral gradient exists, with inner hair cells differentiating prior to their neighboring more laterally located outer hair cells.
source: In addition, a shallower, medial-to-lateral gradient exists, with inner hair cells differentiating prior to their neighboring more laterally located outer hair cells (Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.
